column4: God joins hearts that had been enemies until they become brothers; this is a direct communal counterpart to the section's movement from severed kinship to a joined, merciful people.
Abraham asks God to make this town secure and provide its people with fruits, joining the section's town, sheltering neighbors, and relief from hunger.
Abraham asks that he, his son, and their descendants be made submitting community; lineage becomes a chain of shared faith like the section's tawāṣī.
God chooses Adam, Noah, Abraham's family, and Imran's family, giving the section's parentage and descent a prophetic lineage.
The chosen line is described as descendants of one another; this is a direct formulation of lineage continuing through generations.
Zechariah describes his weakened bones and gray hair; this ayah supplies the old age that makes his successor prayer in 19:5 urgent.
Abraham asks that he and his descendants keep prayer, tying offspring to shared faith and practice.
A pregnant divorced woman must be supported until delivery; if she nurses the child, she is paid and the parents consult honorably, joining birth to mutual care.
The next ayah requires each person to provide according to means, completing 65:6's support for the pregnant mother and child.
The command not to kill children from fear of poverty directly reverses the section's threatened lineage and the needy child's vulnerability.
Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision enact a stark severing of the line the section traces from birth.
The father darkens at news of a daughter and considers hiding her; the ayah shows a family refusing the bond at birth.
He debates keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her in dust; this directly reverses the section's birth and its image of the poor fallen into dust.
The Messenger removes burdens and shackles from people; this is a direct reversal of the section's bound neck and its act of freeing a raqaba.
The ayah asks whether the opponent knows that God sees him, a direct formulation of the section's challenge to the man who thinks nobody saw him.
God joins believers' hearts when no wealth could have united them; this makes the section's joining of separate people into a community concrete.
On the Day the Trumpet is blown, there are no family ties among them; this marks a boundary to the lineage bond the section traces.
On that Day a person flees from his brother, a stark reversal of the section's companion and joined-kin images.
The same person flees from his mother and father, showing descent bonds failing at Judgment.
He flees from his spouse and children, completing the reversal of the section's family and offspring ties.
No close friend asks after another on that Day; this reverses the section's companion as nearness and protection.
People are made to see one another, completing the scene of estranged companions begun in 70:10.
A person would ransom his children from the punishment, making offspring a desperate attempted rescue rather than the section's continuing lineage.
He would also ransom his spouse and brother, extending the failure of close bonds in 70:10.
He would ransom everyone on earth to save himself, completing the breakdown of family and clan solidarity.
Intimate friends become enemies on that Day except the Godwary; the section's companion and mercy roots find their boundary in faith.
The ayah orders help for enslaved people seeking a freedom contract and aid from God's provision, a concrete social form of releasing the bound neck.
The hand chained to the neck is an image of withholding wealth; the ayah warns against stinginess, reversing the section's freeing of a neck and feeding the needy.
Each person comes alone, leaving wealth and intercessors behind; this directly contrasts the section's isolated orphan and its turn toward companions.
The wealthy claimant is told that his possessions will be inherited and that he will come alone; this directly answers the section's boaster, wealth, descendants, and solitude.
Everyone comes to God individually on the Day of Resurrection, a boundary to the section's collective companionship.
A man nearing death must provide a bequest for his wife; this joins the section's waṣiyya (connected speech) to care for a surviving family member.
A child rebukes parents who call him to faith despite their care; this is the opposite of gratitude for parental labor in the section and in 46:15.
The Prophet's gentleness keeps people from dispersing, and he is told to pardon and consult them; this specifies mercy as a force that holds a community together.
The command to cooperate in righteousness and piety gives the section's mutual connection a practical communal form.
Justice must stand even against parents and near relatives; the section's qarāba (kinship) is a bond, but not a license to abandon justice.
Pharaoh promises successful magicians a place among the near ones; this repeated q-r-b wording makes nearness a worldly favor, unlike the section's faith-based closeness.
People fear being snatched from their land if they follow guidance, while God has established a secure sanctuary and provision; this connects the section's town and neighboring life to safety.
Adam and his wife are told to dwell together in the Garden; the section's dictionary form of miskin derives from s-k-n, settling toward a beloved, and this ayah gives that rest a domestic scene.
The same command to dwell in the Garden is addressed to Adam and his wife, repeating the section's s-k-n link between rest and companionship.
Homes are made a sakan (resting place); this Qur'anic sense of the section's miskin root links shelter to the family home.
God sends sakīna into believers' hearts to increase their faith; the section describes faith as calm and the departure of fear.
At the pledge under the tree, God sends tranquility into believers' hearts; this is another communal instance of faith settling fear.
God sends tranquility on the Messenger and believers and binds them to piety, joining faith and calm in a community.
After the believers are shaken in battle, God sends tranquility upon them; this directly illustrates faith's removal of fear.
The disbelievers are described with fetters around their necks, the opposite of the section's freeing a bound neck.
Fetters reach the disbelievers' chins and hold their heads raised; this is a specific reversal of releasing the neck.
The condemned are dragged with shackles around their necks, a direct contrary scene to freeing the neck in the section.
